---
title: "One writer (`&mut T`) xor Many Reader (`&T`)"
---

Borrowing is where Rust's design really clicks, because the "one writer or many readers" rule turns out to be a single idea that prevents several different classes of bugs at once. Let's build it up.

---

## 1. Recap: what a borrow is

From last time: an owner holds the "free this" duty. A borrow (a reference) is a pointer that lets you use the value without taking that duty. Rust has exactly two kinds:

```
 ┌──────────────┬────────────────────────┬──────────────┬────────────────────┐
 │ Syntax       │ Common name            │ Can mutate?  │ How many at once?  │
 ├──────────────┼────────────────────────┼──────────────┼────────────────────┤
 │ &T           │ shared reference       │ No           │ As many as you like│
 │ &mut T       │ mutable reference      │ Yes          │ Exactly ONE, and   │
 │              │                        │              │ no &T alongside it │
 └──────────────┴────────────────────────┴──────────────┴────────────────────┘
```

The names `&` and `&mut` are slightly misleading. The more accurate mental names are shared vs exclusive (or unique). The real meaning of `&mut` is "nobody else can touch this right now"; mutation is just the thing exclusivity makes safe.

The rule in one line:

```
        ALIASING  XOR  MUTATION
   (many can see it)   (it can change)
          you may have one or the other, never both at the same time
```

## 2. What the owner itself may do while a borrow exists

Borrowing also restricts the owner, which surprises people at first:

```
 ┌───────────────────────────┬──────────────┬───────────────┬──────────────┐
 │ While the value has...    │ Owner reads? │ Owner writes? │ Owner moves? │
 ├───────────────────────────┼──────────────┼───────────────┼──────────────┤
 │ no borrows                │ ✓            │ ✓ (if mut)    │ ✓            │
 │ one or more &T borrows    │ ✓            │ ✗             │ ✗            │
 │ one &mut T borrow         │ ✗            │ ✗             │ ✗            │
 └───────────────────────────┴──────────────┴───────────────┴──────────────┘
```

```rust
let mut s = String::from("hi");
let m = &mut s;          // exclusive access handed to m
println!("{s}");         // error[E0502]: cannot borrow `s` as immutable
                         //               because it is also borrowed as mutable
m.push('!');
```

Even the owner can't peek while someone else holds the exclusive borrow. That's what "exclusive" means.

## 3. Why the rule exists, part 1: single-threaded invalidation

You might think "if there's only one thread, how could reading while writing ever go wrong?" Here's the canonical example:

```rust
let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3];
let first = &v[0];       // shared borrow pointing INTO v's heap buffer
v.push(4);               // error[E0502]: cannot borrow `v` as mutable
                         //               because it is also borrowed as immutable
println!("{first}");
```

It looks harmless, but `push` may need more capacity. When it does, `Vec` allocates a bigger buffer, copies the elements over, and frees the old one. Step through what would happen if Rust allowed it:

The general pattern is: a reader holds a pointer that assumes the structure stays put, and a writer changes the structure underneath it. The languages you know hit the same problem, but detect it at runtime, if at all:

```
 C#     : foreach (var x in list) list.Add(x);
          → InvalidOperationException: "Collection was modified"   (runtime)
 Python : for k in d: d[k + "x"] = 1
          → RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration  (runtime)
 C++    : for (auto& x : vec) vec.push_back(x);
          → undefined behavior, maybe works, maybe crashes          (silent)
 Rust   : for x in &v { v.push(*x); }
          → error[E0502]                                            (compile time)
```

C# and Python bolt on runtime "version counters" for specific collections. Rust gets the same protection for every type, including your own, from one general rule and with zero runtime cost.

There's a second, subtler benefit. Because `&mut` guarantees no aliasing, the compiler (and you) can reason about code locally:

```rust
fn add_twice(a: &mut i32, b: &i32) {
    *a += *b;
    *a += *b;
}
```

If `a` and `b` could point to the same integer (starting at 1), the result would be 4 instead of the "obvious" 3, because the first line changes what `b` reads. In C this aliasing is legal, so the compiler must reload `*b` every time. In Rust, `add_twice(&mut x, &x)` is a compile error, so the function means exactly what it looks like, and the optimizer can load `*b` once.

## 4. Why the rule exists, part 2: data races

A data race has a precise definition. It occurs when all three of these hold:

```
 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ 1. Two or more threads access the same memory concurrently     │
 │ 2. At least one of them WRITES                                 │
 │ 3. There is no synchronization between them                    │
 └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Points 1 and 2 together are exactly "aliasing plus mutation." So the borrowing rule that protects the `Vec` above is the same rule that rules out data races. Here's why races are so nasty: `counter += 1` is not one operation, it's read, add, write.

```
   counter = 0

   Thread A                 Thread B
   ────────                 ────────
   read  counter → 0
                            read  counter → 0
   add   0 + 1 = 1
                            add   0 + 1 = 1
   write counter ← 1
                            write counter ← 1

   Final: 1   (expected 2)  ← a "lost update", and it only happens sometimes
```

Rust refuses to compile the racy version, because both threads would need a `&mut` to the same value:

```rust
use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let mut counter = 0;
    thread::scope(|s| {
        s.spawn(|| counter += 1);   // closure captures &mut counter
        s.spawn(|| counter += 1);   // error[E0499]: cannot borrow `counter`
    });                             //   as mutable more than once at a time
}
```

Meanwhile, many readers across threads are perfectly fine, because many `&T` is allowed:

```rust
let data = vec![1, 2, 3];
thread::scope(|s| {
    s.spawn(|| println!("{:?}", data));      // &data
    s.spawn(|| println!("{}", data.len()));  // &data
});                                          // ✓ compiles
```

Notice there's no special "threading rule" here. The compiler applied the ordinary borrow rule, and the data race simply couldn't be expressed. (Under the hood, two marker traits, `Send` and `Sync`, decide which types may cross or be shared between threads; most everyday types get them automatically.)

## 5. "But I need shared mutable state!": interior mutability

Real programs sometimes genuinely need several threads updating one counter. Rust's answer is not to break the rule but to enforce it at runtime instead of compile time, using a type that manages exclusivity itself:

```rust
use std::sync::Mutex;
use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let counter = Mutex::new(0);
    thread::scope(|s| {
        for _ in 0..2 {
            s.spawn(|| {
                let mut guard = counter.lock().unwrap(); // wait for exclusivity
                *guard += 1;                             // guard acts like &mut i32
            });                                          // guard dropped → unlock (RAII!)
        }
    });
    println!("{}", counter.into_inner().unwrap()); // always 2
}
```

```
   Both threads hold   &Mutex<i32>        (shared: allowed)
                            │
                  lock() ───┤  only one thread at a time gets through
                            ▼
                   MutexGuard  ≈  &mut i32   (exclusive: still one writer)
```

The "one writer" guarantee still holds; the `Mutex` just checks it while running. And notice how unlocking is handled by `Drop` from last lesson: you can't forget to release the lock. The same family includes `RefCell` (single-threaded, panics if you break the rule at runtime) and atomics like `AtomicUsize` for simple counters. You'll often see `Arc<Mutex<T>>` when the data must outlive a single scope: `Arc` provides shared ownership across threads, `Mutex` provides exclusive access.

## 6. How long does a borrow last?

A borrow lasts from where it's created until its last use, not until the end of the scope. This is called non-lexical lifetimes, and it makes the rules much less annoying in practice:

```rust
let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3];
let first = &v[0];        // ─┐ shared borrow begins
println!("{first}");      // ─┘ last use: borrow ends here
v.push(4);                // ✓ no active borrow, mutation allowed
```

```
   line:        1      2       3       4
   &v (first):         ├───────┤
   &mut v (push):                      ├┤      no overlap → OK
```

The borrow checker is essentially drawing these intervals and making sure a `&mut` interval never overlaps with any other borrow of the same value.

## 7. How this shapes API design

Since you care about architecture: these rules make every function signature a precise contract about what it does with your data, which C# and Python signatures can't express.

```rust
impl Account {
    fn balance(&self) -> i64           // "I only read"        (many callers ok)
    fn deposit(&mut self, amt: i64)    // "I modify, exclusively"
    fn close(self) -> Receipt          // "I consume it; you can't use it after"
}
```

```
   &self       →  like a read-only view; safe to call from many places at once
   &mut self   →  caller must prove nobody else is looking
   self        →  ownership transfer; the old variable is gone (e.g. a builder's
                  .build(), a file's .close(), a state machine's transition)
```

The `self` form is especially powerful for state machines: after `connection.close()`, any later use of `connection` is a compile error, not a runtime "ObjectDisposedException."

## Summary

```
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │  &T      shared     many at once     read-only                       │
 │  &mut T  exclusive  exactly one      read + write, no one else looks │
 │                                                                      │
 │  Core rule:  ALIASING  XOR  MUTATION                                 │
 │                                                                      │
 │  Prevents, with ONE rule, all at compile time:                       │
 │    • iterator / reference invalidation  (single-threaded)            │
 │    • surprising aliasing bugs           (single-threaded)            │
 │    • data races                         (multi-threaded)             │
 │                                                                      │
 │  Need shared mutation?  Mutex / RefCell / atomics enforce the same   │
 │  "one writer" rule at runtime instead.                               │
 │                                                                      │
 │  Borrows last until their LAST USE, not the end of the scope.        │
 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
